findings.where: Phone first screen: the order of the hero's parts (photo, line, address strip, then the 'I advise multilateral development banks…' paragraph)
findings.fault: On a phone the sentence that says what Mark does and for whom comes after the email strip, below the first screen. A visitor gets a photo, a line about PPPs and an email address before learning that he advises development banks and governments. On desktop the order is line, then what he does, then the action, so the phone version is both out of order and inconsistent with desktop.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank staff member opening the link from LinkedIn on a phone. They are asked to write before the page has said what he offers them, and the 5-second test (what is this, for whom) fails on the first screen.

findings.where: Desktop first screen: overall composition (text block left, portrait slab right, about 60/40)
findings.fault: The hero is the stock split template: headline and paragraph on the left, a head-and-shoulders photo filling the right. Only a 1 px frame and a yellow strip set it apart. Round 1's critics already named the 'template split' as something to avoid, and the founder asked for a look no generic consultancy could own, alive rather than dull.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first. He rejected round 1's v5 as fine parts put together dully, and his personal-advisor test fails a look any consultancy could own.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Download' block at the article's foot
findings.fault: A 'Download' label at the end of the 'World's Best PPP Law' blog post offers a different item, a 2026 lecture on 'Abundance'. Nothing says it is related reading. Readers expect a download under an article to be that article, and the 'PDF' tag means the link opens the file directly rather than a page about the lecture.
findings.who_objects: A reader who wants to keep or forward this article. They click expecting the post as a PDF and get an unrelated lecture file. It also cuts against the house rule that each talk gets its own page before its PDF.

findings.where: Article specimen, desktop: the download link's meta line 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: The meta line is pushed to the far right edge of the column, level with the title's first line, with a wide empty gap between them. It reads as a separate right-hand note rather than the type and date of the link it describes.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning for date and format. Proximity ties the meta to empty space, not to the title, and it is easy to miss that the link is a PDF.

findings.fault: The parts map shows this is a button that acts in place, but it wears the link treatment (blue, underlined) that the page reserves for links: the address and the download. The same look stands for two functions.
findings.who_objects: A visitor, or the founder reviewing the tile, who reads it as a link and expects to be taken somewhere. It also sets a precedent that would carry into the build's buttons.

findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law'
findings.fault: The display title uses a straight typewriter apostrophe, while the body and the subhead use curly typographer's quotes (‘chapter topics’, “Not yet!”). At display size the straight mark is conspicuous.
findings.who_objects: A reader with an eye for setting, and Mark, whose look claims 'the editorial gravitas of a legal journal'. A straight apostrophe in the largest line of the article undercuts that.

findings.where: Desktop first screen: the portrait panel's backdrop against the ivory paper
findings.fault: The palette notes say photographs are multiplied onto the paper so their light backdrops take its warmth. In the render the studio backdrop stays a cool flat grey, so about 40% of the first screen reads as a grey slab beside the warm ivory rather than one sheet of paper.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging 'the exact colours and shades' of a legal-pad direction. The promised warm, single-ground sheet is not what the first screen shows.
